t: Why Difficult Students Need Your Unconditional Acceptance nal-acceptance/
q: Effective classroom management requires you to hold difficult students accountable beyond just the four walls of your classroom.
Everyone on campus knows who they are and are quick to point out their transgressions.
Thinking too much, too often, and too critically about one's performance can cause unrelenting stress and anxiety. It causes athletes to freeze up, salespeople to fumble their presentations.
Simply following your classroom management plan is enough for her to understand that she made a mistake.
She needs to know that her mistakes don’t define her and that even if she were to mess up every single day, you would still be in her corner and on her side.
Your most difficult students need not your red-faced lectures or your bitter disappointment, but your forgiveness, your grace, and your unconditional acceptance.

t: How To Handle A Student Who Habitually Calls Out https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2013/05/11/how-to-handle-a-student-who-habitually-calls-out/
q: Namely, how do you deal with a student who, despite receiving consequence after consequence, continues to call out in class?
Like a lion cub that doesn’t get enough to eat, she has learned that she must assert herself or get pushed to the margins.
She also needs to know that you will never respond to her when she calls out. Hearing this plainly and clearly from you will relieve a good deal of the internal stress that is causing the habit.
Instead, make brief but pleasant eye contact with her (2-3 seconds) and then call on someone else.
When you do notice her sitting quietly with her hand raised—and you will—casually call on her like you would any other student.
Responding to students who call out is the very thing that encourages it—along with encouraging a host of other disruptive behavior.
x: Responding to reader questions, Linsin outlines a compassionate, multi-step approach for a student—often new to the class—who habitually calls out despite repeated consequences.
He frames chronic call-outs as often originating in a previous classroom where calling out was the only way to be heard, likening the student to 'a lion cub that doesn't get enough to eat.'
Step 2: prove it by never responding to a call-out, even briefly, since answering even once reinforces the habit for her and others.

The plan involves privately assuring the student that raising her hand guarantees she'll be heard, proving this by never responding to call-outs, making brief but non-responsive eye contact when she calls out anyway…
Step 1: privately assure the student that raising her hand guarantees she'll be called on—and that call-outs will never be answered.

t: How To Avoid An Increase In Misbehavior As The School Year Winds Down s-the-school-year-winds-down/
q: It’s common for behavior to worsen during the final few weeks of the school year.
Sensing summer break approaching, students begin to feel their age outpacing their grade level. They grow restless and excitable.
Knowing that a downward trending of behavior is a possibility, it’s smart to reaffirm your classroom management plan before the dip occurs.
It’s best to reteach your plan as a refresher rather than an angry response.
With testing in the review mirror, many students will conclude that the school year is essentially over, which is a surefire predictor of misbehavior.
Reach the finish line, not with the exhausted, salt-encrusted visage of a marathon runner, but with a sprinter's bounce in your step.
